balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Grab Holdings Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Grab Holdings Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Grab Holdings Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

mtu.title: Monthly Transacting Users (MTU)
mtu.content:
MTU is the number of unique users who completed at least one transaction (a ride, delivery or financial-services use) across Grab's platform in a month, averaged over the period.

For Grab Holdings Limited: MTU is the super-app's equivalent of DAU for a social network -- it is the base revenue, GMV and Financial Services lending all scale from, and it is what cross-sell (On-Demand to Financial Services) depends on.

What to watch:

  • MTU growth decelerating faster than GMV growth (frequency rising instead of reach)
  • MTU growth versus incentive spend (ConsumerIncentives/PartnerIncentives) -- paid growth is not the same as organic

gmvSegment.title: GMV by segment
gmvSegment.content:
GMV (Gross Merchandise Value) is the total value of transactions flowing through the platform before Grab's take rate -- shown here split between Deliveries (food and grocery) and Mobility (ride-hailing); together with Financial Services these make up On-Demand GMV.

For Grab Holdings Limited: Deliveries overtook Mobility in GMV during the pandemic and has stayed larger since -- the mix matters because take rates and margins differ by segment.

What to watch:

  • Which segment is driving the GMV growth in a given quarter
  • GMV growth versus revenue growth (take-rate trend, promoted as the blended GMV column)

gmvPerMtu.title: On-Demand GMV per MTU
gmvPerMtu.content:
On-Demand GMV per MTU is On-Demand (Deliveries + Mobility) GMV divided by Monthly Transacting Users -- a frequency/spend proxy independent of the user-count tailwind.

For Grab Holdings Limited: this is the "are existing users doing more" lens; MTU growth alone can mask falling per-user engagement if incentives are being pulled back.

What to watch:

  • Rising per-MTU GMV alongside slowing MTU growth (maturing cohort, less reliant on incentives)
  • A fall coinciding with lower ConsumerIncentives -- demand elasticity to subsidy

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
Revenue split across Grab's three reporting segments: Mobility (ride-hailing commissions), Deliveries (food/grocery commissions and advertising) and Financial Services (lending, payments and digital banking interest income).

For Grab Holdings Limited: Financial Services is the smallest segment by revenue but the fastest-growing, as the digital bank (GXS/GXBank) scales its loan book -- see LoanReceivables and CustomerDeposits elsewhere on this dashboard.

What to watch:

  • Financial Services revenue growth rate versus the other two segments
  • Mobility revenue recovering versus pre-pandemic levels

segmentEbitda.title: Segment Adjusted EBITDA
segmentEbitda.content:
Adjusted EBITDA by segment -- the clearest view of where Grab is profitable today and where it is still investing. Mobility has been profitable for several years; Deliveries turned profitable more recently; Financial Services has run a structural loss while it builds its loan book and deposit base.

For Grab Holdings Limited: group Adjusted EBITDA turning positive was driven almost entirely by Mobility and Deliveries -- Financial Services' losses are the main drag still being absorbed, and its narrowing (or, in Q3 2026, turning positive) is the next profitability catalyst.

What to watch:

  • Financial Services loss narrowing on a rising loan book (operating leverage, not just slower growth)
  • Mobility/Deliveries margin giving back gains to fund Financial Services' growth

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Grab Holdings Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Grab Holdings Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
